newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania to reopen airport, face down rebel threat.
newsitem.headline: Albania to reopen airport, face down rebel threat.

text.p: Albanian authorities pledged to reopen Tirana airport on Thursday and to face down an ultimatum from armed rebels holding most of the south of the country for President Sali Berisha to quit.

Truckloads of police were sent to secure Rinas airport, 25 km (15 miles) west of Tirana. The airport is Albania's main gateway to the outside world and staging point for any flow of aid to put Albania on its feet after a month of unrest.

Late into Wednesday evening four tanks patrolled Tirana's city centre in the biggest show of force staged by the government since they were first ordered onto streets last week to staunch the threat of violence engulfing the capital. Sporadic shots rang out in city streets.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, in a statement broadcast on state television, urged Albanians to support his all-party government appointed last week and snuff out unrest.

"Let's join forces to support the police, army and local government to solve our problems," he said. "The government will be merciless and strike with the force of law against organised crime and groups terrorising Albanian families."

The government this week said police and troops would be deployed to allow the resumption of commercial flights halted last Thursday, when police and the army deserted their posts. Army depots were looted throughout the country.
Italian military helicopters landed at Rinas on Wednesday to bring back nearly 300 people authorities in Rome said were criminals using the confusion to flee to Italy.
Although Tirana has been relatively calm since last weekend, Western airlines said they had no intention of resuming operations until at least Sunday.
This week's rebel ultimatum said the revolt's leaders would constitute a presidential council in southern regions under their control if Berisha did not step down by Thursday.
But leaders of the government, charged with overseeing new elections in June, said calls for Berisha's resignation were a threat to the country's fragile post-communist institutions.

"If President Berisha gives in to such a request...a constitutional vacuum would be created in Albania," Albanian Foreign Minister Arjan Starova told a news conference in Rome alongside Italian opposite number Laberto Dini. "That's not good for the country."
Fino urged the rebels to lay down their weapons and support his government against "those trying to sow chaos and terror".

Well over 100 people have died in the revolt triggered by the failure of dubious investment schemes which swallowed up the life savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians. Most victims were killed by stray bullets fired from looted guns.
Clashes have persisted in several towns, with at least 14 deaths recorded in the last two days.

Berisha was re-elected by parliament last month, but has been accused by rebels of failing to check the spread of the fraudulent investment schemes. He has also been criticised for the conduct of last year's parliament elections, won by his Democratic Party but viewed as unfair by Western observers.
A European Union (EU) mission probing how to put the country of 3.4 million back on its feet said restoring order and confidence in security forces were vital to aid programmes.
A state of emergency remains in place, with an overnight curfew, the shutdown of schools and publishing restrictions which have shut down nearly all newspapers.
Finance Minister Arben Malaj told state television Albania faced "complete financial paralysis" and was in no position to pay for hospitals, education and the security forces.

In Washington, NATO commander General George Jouwlan said he saw few parallels between the unrest in Albania and ethnic warfare in nearby Bosnia. "It's lawlessness, it's criminal, it's a very poor country, but I don't see it evolving into another Bosnia," he told a congressional hearing.

But in Italy, the unrest and the more than 10,000 refugees it has sent fleeing across the Adriatic prompted the government to introduce a "state of emergency" -- intended mainly to free funds to cope with the influx.
